subject: research/flex-twin
professional: a senior motion-control / structural-dynamics engineer (servo drives, flexible manipulators). They would check first that the two-mass closed-loop polynomial is right for load-side vs motor-side sensing, that the stability boundary agrees with an eigenvalue computation, whether the delta/zeta limit is already known (non-collocated control of a lightly damped mode: Gevarter 1970, Cannon & Schmitz 1984, Preumont), and whether 'ordinary validation gives no warning' survives a frequency-response (sine-sweep / Bode) validation

evidence.correctness: Derived both closed-loop polynomials by hand from the transfer functions x2/u=(cs+k)/(s^2(J1J2 s^2+cMs+kM)) and x1/u=(J2s^2+cs+k)/(...): both match coeffs() (model.py:20-24) and the normalised quartic; expanded the third Hurwitz minor by hand and it reduces exactly to -4e*cubic (model.py:66); evaluated cubic(delta/zeta) symbolically: d^5(1/z^3-4/z)+d^3(2/z-4z), = -2*sqrt2*d^5 at z=1/sqrt2 as claimed. Independent numerics (indep.py: state matrix from Newton's laws, numpy eigvals, scipy brentq on max Re, scipy lsim): eps_c = 0.071415910590 for all five mu (identical to 12 digits), the full 6x3 eps_c table identical to 5 digits, delta=0 has max Re > 0 at every eps tried, 7320 collocated grid points all with max Re < 0 (worst -9.9e-13), step-response gaps 2.336e-05 / 2.103e-03 / 6.247e-03 and peak 1.0485 and ts 94.6 identical to RK4, 1.1 eps_c diverges. Extended beyond the paper's grid (delta 0.3-1.0, zeta 0.3-1.0): the stable eps set is always one interval and eps_c equals the unique positive cubic root. Every number reproduces; run.py rerun is byte-identical to results.txt.
evidence.completeness: README promises: 9 tests <1 s (Ran 9 tests in 0.672s OK), run.py about 20 s reproducing results.txt (real 21.3 s, byte-identical diff), figure.py regenerates critical_bandwidth.svg (identical in a scratch copy), live page https://marisstella.app/research/flex-twin/ (HTTP 200, title 'How high a bandwidth does a rigid-body twin...', figure linked). All six results in the whitepaper are produced by run.py sections 1-6. Notch, delta identification, sampling delay, multi-mode are honestly Next steps. Unused path: simulate(collocated=True) is never exercised by run.py or tests.
evidence.verification: cd research/flex-twin && PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v: 9 OK. Five mutants via platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: 3 caught (Hurwitz a3^2 a0 -> a3 a0; damper c scaled 1.01; settle_time off by one step), 2 SURVIVED: the collocated a2 coefficient kp*J2 -> kp*J1 (model.py:23; the only collocated test asserts 'always stable', which a wrong polynomial also satisfies, so result 3 is not tested against physics) and the twin simulation's inertia M -> 1.05 M (model.py:93; changes every section-4 number, nothing pins results.txt). No test compares any polynomial to an eigenvalue computation.
evidence.craft: Read src/flex_twin/model.py (121 lines), tests/test_model.py, experiments/run.py, figure.py. Stdlib only, small pure functions, docstrings carry the derivation, figure parsed from results.txt. Defects: params() takes (1-4mu)**0.5 with no check, so mu > 0.25 returns complex inertias and real_stable raises "TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'complex' and 'complex'" (model.py:29); eps_crit's hi=100 and the 1e-6 probe are magic numbers; simulate's collocated branch is dead in practice; run.py duplicates the test's 'early/late' growth heuristic rather than sharing it.
evidence.claims: Checked against results.txt and my recomputation: mu-independence, 1.7e-16 agreement, the delta/zeta table, delta=0 instability, 7320/0 collocated, step gaps and settling times, sim-vs-Routh growth, the f/m table: all backed. Wrong: README:3 says the law is 'exact to O(delta^5) at zeta = 1/sqrt2: 0.0143, 0.0714, 0.286 of ws'; those are the zeta = 0.7 values; at 1/sqrt2 they are 0.0141, 0.0707, 0.2844. whitepaper:15 cites '(1.0027 at delta = 0.2)' as the accuracy at zeta = 1/sqrt2; 1.0027 is the zeta = 0.7 column, at 1/sqrt2 the ratio is 1.0055 (the served page correctly says zeta = 0.7). README:3 'ordinary validation gives no warning' is stronger than whitepaper:17, which concedes a validation exciting the mode would see it; a frequency-response test (the standard servo commissioning step) is not tested. Limitations and stylised disclaimer present on README, paper and page.
evidence.fitness: Job: a researcher or controls engineer wanting a quantitative rule for how far a rigid-body twin can be trusted on a flexible-joint plant. The note gives a clean, exactly-derived rule (zeta*w < delta*ws), reproducible in 20 s with no dependencies, which someone could extend. But the nearest prior work on non-collocated control of lightly damped modes (Gevarter 1970, AIAA J. 8(4); Spector & Flashner 1990; the non-collocated chapter of Preumont) is not compared against, so whether delta/zeta is new or a restatement of the first-order modal-perturbation result is not established; no hardware or identified plant; not part of any programme in research/PROGRAMMES.md (grep finds no entry). Sound short note, well short of the PhD-programme bar.
evidence.domain: Against classical servo practice (Routh-Hurwitz, two-mass benchmark of Spong 1987, Preumont collocation argument): the plant, sensing and normalisation are right and the cubic is derived correctly. Departures a practitioner would raise: pure PD with ideal load velocity and no roll-off filter (any real loop has one and it changes the phase at ws); validation strawmanned as step-response matching, whereas commissioning normally checks loop gain/phase margins by a sine sweep, which would show the resonance; collocated stability shown on a grid when a short passivity proof exists. Limits are disclosed, so a controls engineer would sign off on the analysis as stated.

defects.what: README attributes the zeta = 0.7 worked values (0.0143, 0.0714, 0.286) to zeta = 1/sqrt2, where they are 0.0141, 0.0707, 0.2844; whitepaper:15 likewise cites 1.0027 as the law's accuracy at delta = 0.2 for zeta = 1/sqrt2 when it is 1.0055 there (1.0027 is the zeta = 0.7 column)
whitepaper's '(1.0027 at delta = 0.2)' follows the O(delta^5) statement for zeta = 1/sqrt2 but is the zeta = 0.7 value; at 1/sqrt2 it is 1.0055

Tests do not check the collocated polynomial against physics (a2 kp*J2 -> kp*J1 survives because the only collocated test asserts 'always stable') and nothing pins results.txt (twin inertia scaled 1.05 survives while every section-4 number changes); no test compares a polynomial to an eigenvalue computation

Nearest prior work on non-collocated control of a lightly damped mode is not compared (Gevarter 1970; Spector & Flashner 1990; Preumont's non-collocated chapter), so novelty of the delta/zeta limit is not established; 'ordinary validation gives no warning' is tested only for step responses, not the frequency-response checks used in servo commissioning
params() accepts mu > 1/4 and returns complex inertias; real_stable then raises TypeError comparing complex numbers instead of a clear ValueError

verdict: A small, correct and fully reproducible control note: every number recomputes from an independent eigenvalue model (eps_c = 0.071415910590 for all mass ratios, the 18-entry delta/zeta table, 7320/7320 collocated points stable, step-response gaps to four significant figures) and the cubic and its -2*sqrt2*delta^5 residual check by hand. It misses the bar on claims and verification: the README and whitepaper attribute the zeta = 0.7 worked values and the 1.0027 accuracy figure to zeta = 1/sqrt2 (true values 0.0141/0.0707/0.2844 and 1.0055), 2 of 5 seeded mutants survive because the collocated polynomial is never checked against physics and nothing pins results.txt, and the delta/zeta limit is not compared with the classical non-collocated literature, so its novelty is unestablished.
